title: Extracting parts for Duke Ellington at his house
summary: After the Cotton Club he went home with Duke, taking pages of score and copying out the parts for the whole band, sometimes until morning, and kept doing so after he left.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Uh huh. And I got together with Duke in a kind of writing, you know, like extracting, you know? He'd do the score, and I'd take it home or go to his house with him. He used to have a system that in the Cotton Club, after we got through, we both go to Duke Ellington's house, and while he was writing, he'd finish writing and he'd give me a piece of the score and I would start extracting for the whole band, you know? And he'd keep on the piano and start playing and playing, and when he'd get through, he'd give it back to me. And I would stay there sometimes until -- oh gosh -- eight or nine o'clock in the morning writing. So that's how we got together -- doing all the extractions for Duke Ellington.
Had you ever done that before?

No, no. I did a little bit with my uncle in the Municipal Band, you know, just to practice. I used to do that. But like I said, the music came out very easy for me, so I used to do extractions which Duke Ellington used to write -- you know music, too, yourself?

All concert, you know? Like writing one thing -- he'd write for the four saxaphones and the three trumpets and the three trombones, and I got to go there and I would extract them and transpose the whole thing for the band.

I have heard a couple of people say that Duke writes, or wrote, in in his own kind of 'shorthand' musically, and that you really had to know the way Duke did it, and that anybody who could normally read music would not understand how to extract for Duke. Is that right?

Well, in a way, that is right. But it's a case that hardly anybody extracted for Duke except Tom Whale or myself. But I did most of the extraction; for Duke, I did all of the extraction myself, because we did it with pencil, no ink or nothing.
I remember seeing you work with Duke, you know, later, in later years, but even after you were no longer with the band, you were still doing extracting for Duke.
Because I remember when Duke was working on the score for Assault on a Queen, and you were over at the hotel extracting as fast as he wrote.
Oh, he came in here one day, he came in here one day and brought me the score for something -- I forgot what it was, but I did a lot of work for Duke -- very much work.
